tool.name: SimpleTPI
tool.summary: Computes the Topographic Position Index (TPI) of a DEM over a neighborhood: each cell's elevation minus the mean elevation of the cells around it. Positive values sit above their surroundings (ridges, hills); negative values sit below (valleys, channels). Choose any of five outputs: raw TPI in elevation units, TPI standardized (in standard-deviation units) at neighborhood scale or at DEM scale, TPI in percentile units, or an experimental TPI standardized by the neighborhood standard deviation of TPI. Computed internally (no Spatial Analyst extension).

usage.para: The Topographic Position Index (Weiss 2001, after Guisan et al. 1999) is the difference between a cell's elevation and the average elevation of a neighborhood around it. It is the raw ingredient behind the Slope Position and Landform Classification tools, and is useful on its own as a continuous measure of where a cell sits on the landscape: strongly positive on ridges and hilltops, strongly negative in valleys and channels, near zero on flats and on even mid-slopes. Several standard terrain-position metrics of Wilson and Gallant (2000) are offered as outputs.

NEIGHBORHOOD SIZE IS THE SPATIAL SCALE OF THE ANALYSIS. TPI is inherently scale-dependent: the same point can read as a valley at one scale and a hilltop at another, and both are valid. A small neighborhood captures small, local hills and hollows; a large neighborhood captures broad ridges and valleys. Choose the scale that matters for your question. The neighborhood may be a circle (all cells within the radius) or an annulus (a ring between an inner and outer radius; the shape Weiss's own examples used), with the radius given in cells or ground units. The neighborhoods are computed exactly, avoiding the cell-rounding quirks of some focal-statistics tools, and NoData cells are ignored in the neighborhood mean.
FIVE OPTIONAL OUTPUTS (choose any combination):
1. TPI in elevation units -- the raw TPI, each cell's elevation minus the mean elevation of its neighborhood, in the DEM's own vertical units:
diff = elevation - (mean elevation of the neighborhood)

Absolute relief: a 100 m hill reads as roughly +100 wherever it occurs, which is usually the most appropriate form for ecological and wildlife questions. This is Wilson and Gallant's (2000) "diff" (equation 3.27); see also Weiss (2001).

2. TPI standardized at neighborhood scale -- the raw TPI divided by the standard deviation of elevation within each cell's own neighborhood, in standard-deviation units (0 where the neighborhood is flat):
dev = ( elevation - neighborhood mean elevation ) / ( neighborhood standard deviation of elevation )

It makes a cell's value relative to the variability of its immediate surroundings, so identical relief can read differently in smooth versus rough terrain. This is Wilson and Gallant's (2000) "dev" (equation 3.30); see also Weiss (2001).
3. TPI in percentile units -- for each cell, the count of neighborhood elevations less than the focal elevation, as a percentage of the neighborhood:
pctl = 100 x ( count of neighborhood elevations less than the focal elevation ) / ( number of cells in the neighborhood )

Values near 0 indicate the cell's elevation is relatively very low compared with its neighbors; values near 100 indicate it is relatively high. Note that this output typically takes much longer to compute than the others -- it must compare every cell against all of its neighbors, so its running time grows with the neighborhood size. This is Wilson and Gallant's (2000) "pctl" (equation 3.31).
4. TPI standardized at DEM scale -- the elevation standardized over the whole raster, in standard-deviation units (dimensionless):
( elevation - DEM mean elevation ) / ( DEM standard deviation of elevation )
This is neighborhood-independent -- it simply expresses how high or low each cell sits within the entire DEM's elevation distribution -- and is likely the least-used of the outputs. See Weiss (2001).
5. TPI standardized by neighborhood SD of TPI (experimental) -- the raw TPI divided by the standard deviation of the raw TPI values within each cell's own neighborhood:
dev_tpi = ( elevation - neighborhood mean elevation ) / ( neighborhood standard deviation of the TPI values )

Unlike output 2 (which divides by the standard deviation of ELEVATION), this divides by the standard deviation of the TPI itself, expressing each cell's position relative to the local roughness of the terrain-position surface rather than the local relief. It is offered for exploration and is NOT part of Wilson and Gallant (2000). Caveat: it is numerically unstable on smooth or planar slopes, where the TPI is near zero AND its neighborhood standard deviation is near zero (a 0/0 that amplifies noise) -- which is why it is offered only here and is deliberately excluded from the Slope Position and Landform Classification tools; the elevation-based neighborhood-standardized output (2) stays well behaved in those areas.

Each output is a floating-point raster with statistics, a histogram, and a diverging blue (below / low) to white to red (above / high) stretch. Everything is computed in numpy with no Esri Con or Spatial Analyst.

References: Weiss, A. 2001. Topographic Position and Landforms Analysis. Poster presentation, ESRI User Conference, San Diego, CA (http://www.jennessent.com/arcview/TPI_Weiss_poster.htm). Wilson, J. P., and J. C. Gallant. 2000. Terrain analysis: principles and applications. John Wiley and Sons (equations 3.27, 3.30, and 3.31). Guisan, A., S. B. Weiss, and A. D. Weiss. 1999. GLM versus CCA spatial modeling of plant species distribution. Plant Ecology 143:107-122 (https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1009841519580). Jenness, J. 2006. Topographic Position Index (tpi_jen.avx) extension for ArcView 3.x (http://www.jennessent.com/arcview/tpi.htm).

dialogReference.para: The elevation raster (DEM), single band. Projected and geographic (latitude/longitude) coordinate systems are both supported; on a geographic DEM a ground-unit radius is sized per row on the spheroid, so it changes with Latitude in order to maintain a true circle on the ground.

Optional. The raw TPI: each cell's elevation minus the mean elevation of its neighborhood, in the DEM's elevation units. Absolute relief -- a 100 m hill reads as roughly +100 wherever it occurs, usually the most appropriate form for ecological and wildlife questions. A name is suggested from the input. Leave any output blank to skip it; at least one of the five outputs is required.

This statistic is Wilson and Gallant's (2000) "diff" (equation 3.27). References: Wilson, J. P., and J. C. Gallant. 2000. Terrain analysis: principles and applications. John Wiley and Sons. Weiss, A. 2001. Topographic Position and Landforms Analysis. Poster presentation, ESRI User Conference, San Diego, CA (http://www.jennessent.com/arcview/TPI_Weiss_poster.htm).

param.name: out_dev
param.displayname: Output TPI, standardized at neighborhood scale (std. deviations)

dialogReference.para: Optional. TPI standardized at neighborhood scale: (elevation - neighborhood mean elevation) / neighborhood standard deviation of elevation, in standard-deviation units (0 where the neighborhood is flat). It makes a cell's value relative to the variability of its immediate surroundings.

This statistic is Wilson and Gallant's (2000) "dev" (equation 3.30). References: Wilson, J. P., and J. C. Gallant. 2000. Terrain analysis: principles and applications. John Wiley and Sons. Weiss, A. 2001. Topographic Position and Landforms Analysis. Poster presentation, ESRI User Conference, San Diego, CA (http://www.jennessent.com/arcview/TPI_Weiss_poster.htm).

Optional. TPI in percentile values within the neighborhood. Value calculated as the count of elevation values in the neighborhood less than the focal elevation, divided by the number of cells in the neighborhood, then multiplied by 100:
pctl = 100 x ( count of neighborhood elevations less than the focal elevation ) / ( number of cells in the neighborhood )
Values near 0 indicate the elevation is relatively very low compared with its neighbors; values near 100 indicate the elevation is relatively high.
Note: this output typically takes much longer to compute than the others -- it must compare every cell against all of its neighbors, so its running time grows with the neighborhood size.
This statistic is Wilson and Gallant's (2000) "pctl" (equation 3.31). Reference: Wilson, J. P., and J. C. Gallant. 2000. Terrain analysis: principles and applications. John Wiley and Sons.

param.name: out_demstd
param.displayname: Output TPI, standardized at DEM scale (std. deviations)

dialogReference.para: Optional. TPI standardized over the whole raster: (Elevation - DEM Mean Elevation) / DEM Standard Deviation, in standard-deviation units (dimensionless). This is neighborhood-independent -- it expresses how high or low each cell sits within the entire DEM's elevation distribution -- and is likely the least-used of the outputs.
Reference: Weiss, A. 2001. Topographic Position and Landforms Analysis. Poster presentation, ESRI User Conference, San Diego, CA (http://www.jennessent.com/arcview/TPI_Weiss_poster.htm).

param.name: out_devtpi
param.displayname: Output TPI, standardized by neighborhood SD of TPI (experimental)

dialogReference.para: Optional and EXPERIMENTAL. The raw TPI divided by the standard deviation of the raw TPI values within each cell's own neighborhood, in standard-deviation units (0 where the neighborhood TPI is uniform):
dev_tpi = ( elevation - neighborhood mean elevation ) / ( neighborhood standard deviation of the TPI values )

Unlike the neighborhood-standardized output (which divides by the standard deviation of elevation), this divides by the standard deviation of the TPI itself, expressing each cell's position relative to the local roughness of the terrain-position surface rather than the local relief.

Caveat: this output is numerically unstable on smooth or planar slopes, where the TPI is near zero AND its neighborhood standard deviation is near zero (a 0/0 that amplifies noise). For that reason it is offered only here, for exploration, and is deliberately excluded from the Slope Position and Landform Classification tools. It is NOT part of Wilson and Gallant (2000).
Circle (all cells within the radius) or Annulus (a ring between an inner and outer radius).
The (outer) neighborhood radius, in the units chosen below. This sets the Spatial Scale (aka Bandwidth), of the analysis -- larger radii capture broader landforms.
For an annulus, the inner radius of the ring (cells nearer than this are excluded). Ignored for a circle.
Cells or a ground unit (Meters, Kilometers, Feet, Miles). A ground-unit radius is converted to a number of cells using the DEM's cell size.

On a geographic (latitude/longitude) DEM the cell size in meters is worked out separately for the east-west (width) and north-south (height) directions -- the east-west width is computed per row on the spheroid and shrinks toward the poles, while the north-south height is essentially constant -- and the radius is converted to a cell count on each axis independently. This produces an elliptical kernel in pixel space that is a true circle on the ground; and because the east-west width changes with Latitude, the horizontal radius (in cells) is recomputed row by row, so the neighborhood stays a true circle on the ground at every latitude.

The DEM's elevation units (Meters or Feet). Detected and locked when the DEM defines a vertical coordinate system. Used only to label the raw TPI output; it does not change the TPI values, which are always in the DEM's own vertical units, and does not affect the standardized (dimensionless) or percentile outputs.

scriptExample.title: Topographic Position Index example (stand-alone script)
scriptExample.para: Raw and neighborhood-standardized TPI from a DEM over a 300 m annulus. The comment block lists every valid choice for the list-driven parameters; pass these strings EXACTLY as shown. All five outputs are optional -- provide any combination (at least one).
scriptExample.code:
import arcpy arcpy.ImportToolbox(r"C:\path\to\JennessEnterprisesTools.pyt") # your installed path is shown in this tool's run messages
# ---- valid options for the list-driven parameters ------------------------ # nb_shape: "Circle" | "Annulus" # nb_units: "Cells" | "Meters" | "Kilometers" | "Feet" | "Miles" # elev_units: "Meters" | "Feet" # outputs (all optional; any combination, at least one): # out_tpi raw TPI (elevation units) # out_dev TPI standardized at neighborhood scale (std. deviations) # out_pctl TPI in percentile units (slow on large neighborhoods) # out_demstd TPI standardized at DEM scale (std. deviations) # out_devtpi TPI / neighborhood SD of TPI (experimental)
arcpy.jenness.SimpleTPI( in_raster="dem.tif", out_tpi="dem_TPI.tif", out_dev="dem_TPI_dev.tif", nb_shape="Annulus", nb_outer=300, nb_inner=100, nb_units="Meters", elev_units="Meters")

dataIdInfo.idPurp: Topographic Position Index of a DEM (elevation minus neighborhood mean) over a circle or annulus, as raw elevation units, standardized (neighborhood-scale or DEM-scale) standard-deviation units, or percentile units (Wilson and Gallant 2000); no Spatial Analyst.
dataIdInfo.idAbs: Computes the Topographic Position Index (Weiss 2001): each cell's elevation minus the mean elevation of a neighborhood (circle or annulus, radius in cells or ground units, NoData-ignoring, geodesic per row on geographic DEMs). Up to four continuous float outputs, following Wilson and Gallant (2000): raw TPI in elevation units (their "diff", eq. 3.27); TPI standardized at neighborhood scale ((elevation - neighborhood mean) / neighborhood SD; their "dev", eq. 3.30); TPI in percentile units (100 x count of neighborhood elevations below the focal / neighborhood count; their "pctl", eq. 3.31); and TPI standardized at DEM scale ((elevation - DEM mean) / DEM SD, whole-raster, neighborhood-independent). Positive/high above the surroundings, negative/low below. Computed in numpy with no Spatial Analyst; each output carries statistics, a histogram, and a blue-white-red diverging stretch. TPI is the ingredient behind the Slope Position and Landform Classification tools.
